cells.tense: You are keeping more than one thing alive right now, and you know which one needs what.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're bringing along and tell the one person who has a stake what you did for it this week.
cells.core:
Whatever's growing in your care is getting what it needs. You feel which one is thirsty and which one wants to be left alone, and you act on it without making a production of it. The work is steady, and it's coming from you.

There's a finish line somewhere in this, and you'll know when it arrives. Nothing here needs to be pried open or let go of early; when the thing is done, releasing it will feel like the point of the work rather than the loss of it. Some of that is worth saying out loud. Name one thing, and one person who has a stake in it, and what you actually did this week — not to be thanked, but so the work stops being invisible.
cells.sheetLine: You know what this needs, and you give it.

cells.tense: You are already living weeks past today, arranging a future that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're bringing along and do nothing to it for a week except look at it once a day.
cells.core:
You've got a picture of where this all ends up, and you're running toward it early. Feeding before the plant asks, correcting before the mistake, planning the harvest while it's still seed. Care that arrives before it's needed starts to feel like pressure, and what you're growing can't tell your hand apart from the conditions it's in.

It doesn't need you to be less devoted. It needs you to trust the pace. Choose one thing you're bringing along, and this week leave it alone except to look. If it grows anyway, you've learned what your part is for; if it doesn't, you'll find that out with time to act. Either way you'll know what you're actually responsible for.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending a crop no one planted yet.
cells.place: at the bench where something is being brought along

cells.tense: You are not bringing anything along right now, and you would say that's not your job.
cells.ask: Put one small living thing where you'll pass it daily and keep it watered for two weeks — that's the whole ask.
cells.core:
There's a stretch of your day where something could be fed, checked, or kept going — and you walk past it. You still notice what's struggling and still know what it needs. You just don't move toward it, and you'd tell anyone it isn't yours to handle. What you know sits there unused.

What's dried up is the doing, not the caring. So start with something that can't disappoint you: a plant on a sill, a seedling, a few herbs you actually water. Two weeks of that and you'll be moving toward it before you decide anything about it. Nothing large, nothing that leans on you yet — just the watering.
cells.sheetLine: You still know what it needs. You don't do it.

cells.tense: You're already tending something in the room, and you're calling it just keeping things running.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been keeping alive without saying so and tell someone what it needs — once, plainly.
cells.core:
Look at what's around you and what's still alive. Something in your daily round gets fed, adjusted, protected — and you do it as reflex, the same way you'd change a lightbulb. You'd name it as maintenance. It's the actual job, and you're the one doing it.

That's not a bad thing, except that nobody knows it's happening, including you. When a thing isn't named, it can't be finished or handed over — it just keeps running quietly. So say the true sentence once, to someone: this needs water, this needs three more weeks, this is the thing that keeps going. Once it's spoken, the work has an owner, and it can end someday. That's the relief, not the risk.
cells.sheetLine: You've been keeping it alive and calling it upkeep.
